claim: Approximately 80% of CD8α+CCR2+ T cells expressed TCRVα7.2 and CD161, identifying them as MAIT cells.
source: We found that approximately 80% of the CD8α+CCR2+ T cells expressed TCRVα7.2 and CD161 (Figure 1A), which identify them as MAIT cells (Martin et al., 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1A and references a citation (Martin et al., 2009) for the identification criteria.

claim: Approximately 75% of MAIT cells were CCR2+.
source: approximately 75% of MAIT cells were CCR2+
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in the manuscript.

claim: MAIT cells prominently expressed CXCR4, CXCR6, CCR5 and CCR6, but lacked CCR7.
source: In addition to CCR2, we found that MAIT cells also prominently expressed CXCR4, CXCR6, CCR5 and CCR6, but lacked CCR7 (Figure 1B), consistent with published data (Dusseaux et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by chemokine receptor expression data shown in Figure 1B and is consistent with published literature (Dusseaux et al., 2011).

claim: CCR6 and CD161 marked virtually identical cells within the CD8α+TCRVα7.2+ subset.
source: we found that CCR6 and CD161 marked virtually identical cells within the CD8α+TCRVα7.2+ subset, so that CCR6 and CD161 could be used interchangeably for identifying MAIT cells (Figure 1C)
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1C demonstrating co-expression patterns.

claim: Among memory-phenotype cells, there was a pattern of progressive increase in numbers of cells rolling, arrested, and transmigrating going from CCR6- conventional to CCR6+ conventional to CCR2-/low MAIT to CCR2+ MAIT cells.
source: among the memory-phenotype cells there was, generally, a pattern of progressive increase in numbers of cells rolling, arrested, and transmigrating going from CCR6- conventional to CCR6+ conventional to CCR2-/low MAIT to CCR2+ MAIT cells (Figure 2A)
evidence: The claim is supported by flow chamber assay data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: MAIT cells were most efficient at the step of arresting.
source: The data showed that the MAIT cells were most efficient at the step of arresting
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of flow chamber assay data showing percentages of rolling cells that arrested.

claim: CCR2+ MAIT cells were particularly effective in the final step of TEM.
source: the CCR2+ MAIT cells were particularly effective in the final step of TEM (Figure 2B)
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 2B showing percentages of arrested cells that transmigrated.

claim: CCR2+ MAIT cells, but not cells from other subsets, were retained in ears that had prior intradermal injection of TNFα and IL-1β.
source: We detected retention of CCR2+ MAIT cells, but not cells from the other subsets, in ears that had had prior intradermal injection of TNFα and IL-1β (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo trafficking data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: TNFα treatment of HUVECs up-regulated E-selectin but not P-selectin.
source: On the HUVECs, we detected up-regulation of E-, but not P-selectin, consistent with published data (Yao et al., 1996)
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data on HUVECs and is consistent with published literature (Yao et al., 1996).

claim: TNFα treatment of HUVECs up-regulated both ICAM-1 and VCAM-1.
source: up-regulation of both ICAM-1 and VCAM-1 (Figure 3A)
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: There was a progressive increase in E-selectin-Fc and P-selectin-Fc staining from naive to CCR6− conventional to CCR6+ conventional to CCR2-/low MAIT to CCR2+ MAIT cells.
source: Staining the T-cell subsets using E-selectin-Fc and P-selectin-Fc chimeric proteins showed a progressive increase in staining from naive to CCR6− conventional to CCR6+ conventional to CCR2-/low MAIT to CCR2+ MAIT cells (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by selectin-Fc binding data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: A similar pattern of progressive increase was seen in staining cells for sLex.
source: A similar pattern was seen in staining the cells for sLex (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data for sLex shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Treating cells with exo-sialidase abolished rolling on TNFα-treated HUVECs.
source: Consistent with the critical role for sLex in mediating rolling, we showed that treating cells with an exo-sialidase, which eliminated staining for sLex (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), abolished rolling on TNFα-treated HUVECs (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing loss of rolling after sialidase treatment, shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Expression of FUT7 and ST3GAL4 were highest in the MAIT cells, particularly in the CCR2+ MAIT cell subset.
source: However, expression of FUT7 and ST3GAL4 were highest in the MAIT cells, and particularly in the CCR2+ MAIT cell subset (Figure 3E)
evidence: The claim is supported by real-time RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Pertussis toxin had no effect on rolling.
source: Pertussis toxin had no effect on rolling
evidence: The claim is supported by flow chamber assay data comparing pertussis toxin-treated and untreated cells.

claim: Pertussis toxin reduced the numbers of arrested memory-phenotype cells by approximately 50%.
source: reduced the numbers of arrested memory-phenotype cells by approximately 50%
evidence: The claim is supported by flow chamber assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Pertussis toxin eliminated TEM.
source: and eliminated TEM (Figure 4A)
evidence: The claim is supported by flow chamber assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: TNFα induced high expression of the genes for CCL2, CCL5, and CCL20 in endothelial cells.
source: TNFα induced high expression of the genes for the CCR2 ligand CCL2, the CCR5 ligand CCL5, and the CCR6 ligand CCL20
evidence: The claim is supported by real-time RT-PCR data on TNFα-treated HUVECs shown in Figure 4B.

claim: CXCL16 was expressed at only a low level in endothelial cells that was not augmented by TNFα.
source: whereas CXCL16 was expressed at only a low level that was not augmented by TNFα (Figure 4B)
evidence: The claim is supported by real-time RT-PCR data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Anti-CCL20 antibody significantly reduced numbers of cells arresting in the three CCR6+ subsets.
source: Anti-CCL20 antibody significantly reduced numbers of cells arresting in the three CCR6+ subsets.
evidence: The claim is supported by flow chamber assay data with anti-CCL20 antibody treatment shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Anti-CCL20 significantly reduced the percentage of rolling cells that arrested in two of the three CCR6+ subsets, but not in the CCR6- cells.
source: Similarly, reflecting the effects specifically on the step of arresting, anti-CCL20 significantly reduced the percentage of rolling cells that arrested in two of the three CCR6+ subsets, but not in the CCR6- cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow chamber assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: BMS CCR2 22 did not diminish the numbers of cells rolling or arrested.
source: BMS CCR2 22 did not diminish the numbers of cells rolling or arrested
evidence: The claim is supported by flow chamber assay data with CCR2 antagonist treatment shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Blocking CCR2 had a profound effect on TEM of the CCR2+ MAIT cells.
source: However, blocking CCR2 had a profound effect on TEM of the CCR2+ MAIT cells (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow chamber assay data with CCR2 antagonist shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The CCR2 inhibitor significantly diminished TEM of the CCR6+ conventional cells.
source: The CCR2 inhibitor also significantly diminished TEM of the CCR6+ conventional cells
evidence: The claim is supported by flow chamber assay data shown in Figure 5A and is consistent with CCR2 expression on a subset of these cells.

claim: Blocking CCR5 had no effect on the numbers of cells rolling, arrested, or transmigrated.
source: Blocking CCR5 had no effect on the numbers of cells rolling, arrested, or transmigrated (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow chamber assay data with CCR5 antagonist shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Among transmigrating CCR2+ MAIT cells, blocking CCR5 significantly prolonged the time between when the cells initiated crawling and initiated TEM.
source: However, among the transmigrating CCR2+ MAIT cells, blocking CCR5 significantly prolonged the time between when the cells initiated crawling and initiated TEM (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Blocking CCR5 had no effect on the time interval between arrest and initiating crawling.
source: There was no effect on the time interval between arrest and initiating crawling.
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse microscopy data analyzing different phases of cell migration.

claim: MAIT cells expressed high levels of CEBPD mRNA and C/EBPδ protein.
source: We found that MAIT cells also expressed high levels of CEBPD mRNA and C/EBPδ
evidence: The claim is supported by real-time RT-PCR and Western blot data shown in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: CEBPD mRNA and C/EBPδ protein could be knocked down using CEBPD siRNAs.
source: and that these could be knocked down using CEBPD siRNAs (Figure 6A and B)
evidence: The claim is supported by real-time RT-PCR and Western blot data after siRNA transfection shown in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: siRNA-mediated knockdown of CEBPD diminished the overall trafficking of MAIT, but not non-MAIT cell subsets in flow chamber assays.
source: siRNA-mediated knockdown of CEBPD diminished the overall trafficking of MAIT, but not non-MAIT cell subsets in the flow chamber assays (Figure 6C)
evidence: The claim is supported by flow chamber assay data comparing control and CEBPD siRNA-treated cells shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Knockdown of C/EBPδ had a significant effect on the rolling step of MAIT cells.
source: Knockdown of C/EBPδ had a significant effect on the rolling step (Figure 6C)
evidence: The claim is supported by flow chamber assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Knockdown of C/EBPδ had a modest, separate effect on firm arrest of the MAIT cells.
source: and a modest, separate effect on firm arrest of the MAIT cells (percentage of rolling cells undergoing arrest)
evidence: The claim is supported by flow chamber assay data analyzing percentages of rolling cells that arrested.

claim: Knocking down C/EBPδ had no consistent, independent effect on TEM in the MAIT cell subsets.
source: Importantly, although knocking down C/EBPδ diminished the numbers of MAIT cells crossing the activated endothelial cells through effects on the initial trafficking steps, knocking down C/EBPδ had no consistent, independent effect on TEM (percentage of arrested cells undergoing TEM) in the MAIT cell subsets (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow chamber assay data analyzing percentages of arrested cells that transmigrated, shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Significantly fewer CCR2+ MAIT cells with knockdown of C/EBPδ could be recovered from inflamed ears compared to controls.
source: As compared to controls, significantly fewer cells with knockdown of C/EBPδ could be recovered from the inflamed ears (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo trafficking data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Knockdown of C/EBPδ decreased surface levels of sLex in MAIT, but not in conventional cells.
source: Knockdown of C/EBPδ decreased surface levels of sLex and decreased expression of FUT7 and ST3GAL4 in MAIT, but not in conventional cells (Figure 7A– C).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7A-C.

claim: Knockdown of C/EBPδ decreased expression of FUT7 in MAIT, but not in conventional cells.
source: Knockdown of C/EBPδ decreased surface levels of sLex and decreased expression of FUT7 and ST3GAL4 in MAIT, but not in conventional cells (Figure 7A– C).
evidence: The claim is supported by real-time RT-PCR data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Knockdown of C/EBPδ decreased expression of ST3GAL4 in MAIT, but not in conventional cells.
source: Knockdown of C/EBPδ decreased surface levels of sLex and decreased expression of FUT7 and ST3GAL4 in MAIT, but not in conventional cells (Figure 7A– C).
evidence: The claim is supported by real-time RT-PCR data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Knockdown of C/EBPδ did not decrease expression of GCNT1.
source: Knockdown of C/EBPδ did not decrease expression of GCNT1 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by real-time RT-PCR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: ChIP detected binding of C/EBPδ within the 5' flanking regions of FUT7 and ST3GAL4, specifically in the MAIT cells.
source: chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) detected binding of C/EBPδ within the 5' flanking regions of these genes, specifically in the MAIT cells (Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP assay data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: C/EBPδ supported the expression of surface CCR6 in MAIT cells.
source: In analyzing the effects of knocking down C/EBPδ on chemokine receptors, we found that C/EBPδ supported the expression of surface CCR6 and CCR6 mRNA (Figure 7E–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry and real-time RT-PCR data shown in Figure 7E-G.

claim: C/EBPδ supported the expression of CCR6 mRNA in MAIT cells.
source: In analyzing the effects of knocking down C/EBPδ on chemokine receptors, we found that C/EBPδ supported the expression of surface CCR6 and CCR6 mRNA (Figure 7E–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by real-time RT-PCR data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: ChIP showed binding of C/EBPδ to CCR6.
source: just as for FUT7 and ST3GAL4, ChIP showed binding of C/EBPδ to CCR6 (Figure 7H).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP assay data shown in Figure 7H.

claim: The effect of knocking down C/EBPδ on the expression of CCR6 was limited to the MAIT cells.
source: Again, the effect of knocking down C/EBPδ on the expression of CCR6 was limited to the MAIT cells, concordant with the pattern of C/EBPδ expression.
evidence: The claim is based on comparing effects of C/EBPδ knockdown across different cell subsets and correlating with C/EBPδ expression patterns.

claim: Knocking down C/EBPδ did not have a notable effect on the expression of CCR2 in the MAIT cells.
source: As shown in Figure 7I, knocking down C/EBPδ did not have a notable effect on the expression of either CCR2 or CCR5 in the MAIT cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by real-time RT-PCR data shown in Figure 7I.

claim: Knocking down C/EBPδ did not have a notable effect on the expression of CCR5 in the MAIT cells.
source: As shown in Figure 7I, knocking down C/EBPδ did not have a notable effect on the expression of either CCR2 or CCR5 in the MAIT cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by real-time RT-PCR data shown in Figure 7I.

claim: FucT-VII is the fucosyltransferase that is critical for synthesis of selectin ligands.
source: FucT-VII is the fucosyltransferase that is critical for synthesis of selectin ligands (Knibbs et al., 1996; Malý et al., 1996; Smithson et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The level of FucT-VII is the determining factor in synthesis of E-selectin ligands.
source: In particular, the level of FucT-VII is the determining factor in synthesis of E-selectin ligands (Knibbs et al., 1996; Ley and Kansas, 2004; Wagers et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: ST3Gal-IV, together with ST3Gal-VI, are the critical enzymes for synthesizing selectin ligands in mice.
source: Among sialyltransferases, ST3Gal-IV (Ellies et al., 2002; Sperandio et al., 2006), together with ST3Gal-VI (Yang et al., 2012), are the critical enzymes for synthesizing selectin ligands in mice
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: ST3Gal-IV is the dominant sialyltransferase in synthesizing selectin ligands on myeloid cells in humans.
source: whereas ST3Gal-IV is the dominant sialyltransferase in synthesizing selectin ligands on myeloid cells in humans (Mondal et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: MAIT cells recognize bacterial metabolites of riboflavin in the context of the non-polymorphic MR1.
source: and recognize bacterial metabolites of riboflavin in the context of the non-polymorphic MR1 (Kjer-Nielsen et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Under homeostatic conditions, MAIT cells are found in the intestinal lamina propria and liver.
source: Under homeostatic conditions, MAIT cells are found in the intestinal lamina propria and liver
evidence: The claim represents established knowledge about MAIT cell distribution.

claim: MAIT cells represent a significant percentage of CD8+, memory-phenotype T cells in human blood.
source: and represent a significant percentage of CD8+, memory-phenotype T cells in human blood
evidence: The claim represents established knowledge about MAIT cell frequency in blood.

claim: MAIT cells exhibit potent antibacterial activity.
source: MAIT cells exhibit potent antibacterial activity and accumulate at sites of bacterial infections (Gold et al., 2010; Le Bourhis et al., 2010; Meierovics et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: MAIT cells accumulate at sites of bacterial infections.
source: MAIT cells exhibit potent antibacterial activity and accumulate at sites of bacterial infections (Gold et al., 2010; Le Bourhis et al., 2010; Meierovics et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Human MAIT cells have generally been identified by their co-expression of TCRVα7.2 and the NK cell marker CD161.
source: Human MAIT cells have generally been identified by their co-expression of TCRVα7.2 and the NK cell marker CD161 (Franciszkiewicz et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature describing standard identification methods.

claim: The vast majority of MAIT cells in human blood are CD8α+.
source: The vast majority of MAIT cells in human blood are CD8α+ (many of which are also CD8βlow)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: MAIT cells are able to make effector cytokines.
source: MAIT cells are able to make effector cytokines, and they contain cytotoxic molecules such as perforin, granulysin and granzymes (Dusseaux et al., 2011; Franciszkiewicz et al., 2016; Le Bourhis et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: MAIT cells contain cytotoxic molecules such as perforin, granulysin and granzymes.
source: MAIT cells are able to make effector cytokines, and they contain cytotoxic molecules such as perforin, granulysin and granzymes (Dusseaux et al., 2011; Franciszkiewicz et al., 2016; Le Bourhis et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: MAIT cells are able to produce effector cytokines both in response to TCR activation and directly in response to cytokines such as IL-18 and IL-12.
source: MAIT cells are able to produce effector cytokines both in response to TCR activation and directly in response to cytokines such as IL-18 and IL-12 (Franciszkiewicz et al., 2016; Jo et al., 2014; Slichter et al., 2016; Ussher et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: MAIT cells are decreased in blood of patients with bacterial pneumonias.
source: In support of such a role, MAIT cells are decreased in blood of patients with bacterial pneumonias, and can be identified in M. tuberculosis-infected lungs (Le Bourhis et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: MAIT cells can be identified in M. tuberculosis-infected lungs.
source: In support of such a role, MAIT cells are decreased in blood of patients with bacterial pneumonias, and can be identified in M. tuberculosis-infected lungs (Le Bourhis et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: CCR6, CCR5, and CCR2 serve sequential and distinct functions in MAIT cell extravasation.
source: Our data suggest that CCR6, CCR5, and CCR2 serve sequential and distinct functions in MAIT cell extravasation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple experimental results showing different roles for each receptor in the extravasation process.

claim: CCL20 is displayed on the surface of TNFα-treated endothelial cells.
source: From our experiments using anti-CCL20 antibodies, we can conclude that CCL20 is displayed on the surface of the TNFα-treated endothelial cells
evidence: The claim is inferred from the effectiveness of anti-CCL20 antibodies in blocking CCR6-mediated arrest.

claim: CCL2 is sequestered in endothelial cell vesicles and only available to CCR2 within T-cell-endothelial cell synapses.
source: and from the work of Shulman et al. (2011), we know that CCL2 is sequestered in endothelial cell vesicles and only available to CCR2 within T-cell-endothelial cell synapses.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The separate roles for CCR6, CCR5, and CCR2 could be the result of anatomic segregation of their chemokine ligands.
source: Taken together, these observations suggest that the separate roles for the receptors could be the result of anatomic segregation of their chemokine ligands, which might be a general feature of the chemokine system that limits functional redundancy.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the observed distinct functions and known ligand localization patterns.

claim: FUT7, ST3GAL4, and CCR6 are direct targets of C/EBPδ.
source: our ChIP data suggest that FUT7, ST3GAL4, and CCR6 are direct targets of C/EBPδ
evidence: The claim is based on ChIP data showing C/EBPδ binding to the promoter regions of these genes.

claim: C/EBPδ's regulation of rolling and firm arrest significantly affected numbers of cells migrating across the activated endothelial cells in the flow chamber assays.
source: Since the multiple steps of extravasation occur sequentially and interdependently, C/EBPδ's regulation of rolling and firm arrest significantly affected numbers of cells migrating across the activated endothelial cells in the flow chamber assays.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the sequential nature of extravasation steps and the observed effects of C/EBPδ knockdown.

claim: The effects documented in the flow chamber assays were the basis for the decreased entry of MAIT cells transfected with CEBPD siRNA into inflamed ears.
source: We presume that the effects that we documented in the flow chamber assays were the basis for the decreased entry of MAIT cells transfected with CEBPD siRNA into inflamed ears.
evidence: The claim is based on inference connecting in vitro and in vivo observations.

claim: C/EBPδ might have a role in regulating CCR2 expression in MAIT cells.
source: These data suggest that our negative results notwithstanding, C/EBPδ might, in fact, have a role in regulating CCR2 expression in MAIT cells.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on published data showing C/EBP binding sites in the CCR2 promoter, despite negative results from knockdown experiments.

claim: Experiments using siRNA knockdown will typically underestimate roles of target genes given that mRNA and protein knockdown are incomplete.
source: Regardless, consideration of these data raises the important point that experiments using siRNA knockdown will typically underestimate roles of target genes given that mRNA and protein knockdown are incomplete both at the level of individual cells and across the heterogeneous population of siRNA-transfected cells.
evidence: The claim represents general knowledge about limitations of siRNA knockdown experiments.

claim: The findings using siRNA knockdown of C/EBPδ reflect the lower limit of the activities of C/EBPδ in supporting expression of the glycosyltransferases and CCR6.
source: Consequently, our findings using siRNA knockdown of C/EBPδ reflect the lower limit of the activities of C/EBPδ in supporting expression of the glycosyltransferases and CCR6, and thereby MAIT cell trafficking.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the known limitations of siRNA knockdown efficiency.

claim: ST3Gal-IV sialylates CXCR2 in mice.
source: Nonetheless, it is of interest that studies in mice have shown that ST3Gal-IV sialylates CXCR2 (Frommhold et al., 2008)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: ST3Gal-IV probably sialylates CCR1 and CCR5 (although not CCR2) in mice.
source: and probably CCR1, and CCR5 (although not CCR2) (Döring et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: For CXCR2, CCR1, and CCR5, sialylation is important for chemokine-dependent activation.
source: For these receptors, sialylation is important for chemokine-dependent activation.
evidence: The claim represents knowledge from published studies on chemokine receptor function.

claim: There is no evidence for sialylation of CCR6.
source: There is no evidence for sialylation of CCR6
evidence: The claim is based on the absence of published evidence.

claim: In addition to a decrease in expression of CCR6, knockdown of C/EBPδ could have led to diminished CCR6 function through loss of ST3Gal-IV-dependent sialylation.
source: but it remains possible that in addition to a decrease in expression of CCR6, knockdown of C/EBPδ could have led to diminished CCR6 function through loss of ST3Gal-IV-dependent sialylation.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a possible mechanism that has not been directly tested.

claim: C/EBPδ is one of six members of the C/EBP family of bZIP transcription factors.
source: C/EBPδ is one of six members of the C/EBP family of bZIP transcription factors, each of which contains a basic DNA-binding domain and a 'leucine zipper' dimerization domain (Ramji and Foka, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature describing the C/EBP family.

claim: In mice, Cebpd is induced in many tissues in response to endotoxin or other inflammatory stimuli, including cytokines such as IL-6 and IL-1.
source: In mice, Cebpd is induced in many tissues in response to endotoxin or other inflammatory stimuli, including cytokines such as IL-6 and IL-1, although expression in these contexts is typically transient (Alam et al., 1992; Balamurugan and Sterneck, 2013; Ko et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Studies in Cebpd knockout mice have demonstrated pleiotropic roles for C/EBPδ, including in multiple models of inflammation and infection.
source: Studies in Cebpd knockout mice have demonstrated pleiotropic roles for C/EBPδ, including in multiple models of inflammation and infection (Yan et al., 2013; Chang et al., 2012; Duitman et al., 2012; Litvak et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: C/EBPδ has been implicated in the acute phase response.
source: C/EBPδ has been implicated in the acute phase response (Alam et al., 1992; Juan et al., 1993; Ray and Ray, 1994)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: C/EBPδ has been implicated in the phenotype and function of macrophages.
source: and in the phenotype and function of macrophages (Balamurugan et al., 2013; Chang et al., 2012; Duitman et al., 2012; Litvak et al., 2009; Maitra et al., 2011; Yan et al., 2013; Litvak et al., 2009; Maitra et al., 2011; Balamurugan et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: C/EBPδ has been suggested to enhance the migration of macrophages into infected lung.
source: Of possible relevance to our own work, C/EBPδ has been suggested to enhance the migration of macrophages into infected lung (Duitman et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: A broader role for C/EBPδ in regulating leukocyte migration in inflammation is suggested by data on the C/EBPδ-mediated induction of chemokines.
source: A broader role for C/EBPδ in regulating leukocyte migration in inflammation is suggested by data on the C/EBPδ-mediated induction of chemokines, including the ligands for CCR6 (Chang et al., 2012) and CCR2 (Ko et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is based on inference from published data showing C/EBPδ regulation of chemokine expression.

claim: C/EBPδ plays a role in the transcriptional response of endothelial cells to inflammatory stimuli.
source: and in the transcriptional response of endothelial cells to inflammatory stimuli (Hogan et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Expression of CEBPD was detected in analyzing the transcriptome of human CD8+CD161+ T cells.
source: In T cells, expression of CEBPD was detected in analyzing the transcriptome of human CD8+CD161+ T cells (Billerbeck et al., 2010), which would have included MAIT cells
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: A bioinformatic analysis of the transcriptome and epigenetic modifications of human CD4+ T cells suggested that C/EBPδ might function as one of the 'master regulators' of TEM differentiation.
source: and a bioinformatic analysis of the transcriptome and epigenetic modifications of human CD4+ T cells suggested that C/EBPδ might function as one of the 'master regulators' of TEM differentiation (Durek et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Kruppel-like factor 2 (KLF2) supports T cell trafficking to lymph nodes versus peripheral tissue by enhancing expression of CD62L and CCR7, and suppressing CXCR3.
source: Another transcription factor that has been described with an effect that is analogous but functionally inverse to C/EBPδ is Kruppel-like factor 2 (KLF2), which supports T cell trafficking to lymph nodes versus peripheral tissue by enhancing expression of CD62L and CCR7, and suppressing CXCR3 (Carlson et al., 2006; Preston et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: SOCS1-mediated inhibition of STATs favors T cell trafficking to lymphoid organs versus peripheral tissue by enhancing expression of CCR7 and suppressing expression of CCR6 and CXCR3.
source: Similarly, SOCS1-mediated inhibition of STATs favors T cell trafficking to lymphoid organs versus peripheral tissue by enhancing expression of CCR7 and suppressing expression of CCR6 and CXCR3 (Yu et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: In contrast to KLF2 and SOCS1, C/EBPδ is a positive regulator supporting the tissue-migrating phenotype.
source: Based on our data, in contrast to these other factors, C/EBPδ is a positive regulator supporting the tissue-migrating phenotype.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing C/EBPδ's role in promoting extravasation-related gene expression.

claim: CCR2+ MAIT cells took the shortest time between arrest and completion of transmigration among the T cell subsets studied.
source: In addition, among those cells that transmigrated, the cells within the CCR2+ MAIT subset took the shortest time between arrest and completion of transmigration.
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse microscopy data analyzing transmigration kinetics.

claim: Naive CD8α+ T cells did not adhere to TNFα-activated HUVECs.
source: Naive CD8α+ T cells did not adhere to the HUVECs
evidence: The claim is supported by flow chamber assay data.

claim: No labeled T cells were detected in non-inflamed ears in the in vivo trafficking experiments.
source: We failed to detect any of these cells in non-inflamed ears.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo trafficking data.

claim: Levels of surface PSGL-1 and CD43 could not explain the pattern of selectin ligand expression among T cell subsets.
source: Levels of surface PSGL-1 and CD43 could not explain the pattern of selectin ligand expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is based on flow cytometry data showing that expression patterns of these proteins did not correlate with selectin ligand expression patterns.

claim: CD44 could not account for the pattern of selectin ligand expression among T cell subsets.
source: CD44 could also not account for the pattern of selectin ligand expression
evidence: The claim is based on flow cytometry data showing that CD44 expression did not correlate with selectin ligand expression patterns.

claim: CD44 was found at somewhat higher levels on the CCR6+ subsets as compared with the naive and CCR6- conventional cells.

claim: Expression of selectin ligands reflects regulation of the genes encoding the limiting glycosyltransferases.
source: In general, expression of selectin ligands reflects regulation of the genes encoding the limiting glycosyltransferases (Ley and Kansas, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature and represents established knowledge.

claim: Patterns of expression of GCNT1, FUT4, FUT6, FUT9, ST3GAL1, 2, 3, and six were unremarkable among the T cell subsets.
source: We found that patterns of expression of GCNT1, encoding core 2 β1,6-N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase-I, FUT4, FUT6, FUT9, ST3GAL1, 2, 3, and six were unremarkable (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by real-time RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: There were no differences in expression of LFA-1, VLA-4, and α4β7 that could explain the differences in efficiencies of arrest among the T cell subsets.
source: As can be inferred from the expression patterns of integrin subunits (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), there were no differences in expression of LFA-1, VLA-4, and α4β7 that could explain the differences in efficiencies of arrest among the subsets.
evidence: The claim is based on flow cytometry data of integrin expression shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: CCR2+ MAIT cells expressed the highest levels of CCR6 among the memory-phenotype subsets.

evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: CCR2+ MAIT cells have higher levels of CCR5 expression than CCR2-/low MAIT cells.

claim: MAIT cells selectively expressed CCAAT/enhancer-binding protein delta (C/EBPδ).
source: MAIT cells selectively expressed CCAAT/enhancer-binding protein delta (C/EBPδ).
evidence: The claim is supported by real-time RT-PCR and Western blot data showing high expression in MAIT cells compared to other T cell subsets.

claim: MAIT cells demonstrate a program for extravasation that includes, in part, C/EBPδ and C/EBPδ-regulated genes.
source: Thus, MAIT cells demonstrate a program for extravasastion that includes, in part, C/EBPδ and C/EBPδ-regulated genes, and that could be used to enhance, or targeted to inhibit T cell recruitment into inflamed tissue.
evidence: The claim is based on the collective experimental data showing C/EBPδ regulation of multiple genes involved in extravasation.
